Personality: Duke Hagen de Gisorou was a ruler known for his high personal virtues and his sincere belief in diversity - "We are all Gisorou and it is our diversity that gives us strength". His famous saying is widely recited, but practice is more complicated than slogans. Hagen spent a lot of time in the royal court of Curona, which gave him a national perspective that other dukes did not have, but also distanced him from his own plain territory - he could now calmly govern North Gisoru (previously an almost independent area due to geographical isolation), but it was difficult to effectively control the hinterland of the plains surrounding the capital, and had to rely on the loyalty of stewards and agents. His personal character was beyond reproach and his devotion to the Lady of the Lake was heartfelt, which gave his orders a special moral weight in front of the nobles of North Gisoru who had been accustomed to self-governance for centuries - but also made him intolerant of some of the traditional customs deeply ingrained in the region. Hagen was a thoughtful ruler who disliked hasty decisions, which was both a strength and a weakness - his prudence saved the duchy in times of crisis, but his hesitation also allowed opportunities to pass when decisive action was required. He approached each region trying to understand its specific needs and traditions, and this tolerance allowed his principality to maintain its fragile unity.
Background: When Hagen inherited the Principality of Gisoru, he inherited a territory composed of four geographically and culturally distinct regions. The founder of the duchy, Beren - the tenth of the Grail Companions of Gilles - was seriously wounded in an ambush in the Ardennes Forest and was led to safety by the apparition of a white stag, an event that is still inscribed on the coat of arms of the ducal family. Hagen knew that he ruled a land divided in culture and loyalties: the plainsmen were known for their hospitality but sharp boundaries, the Ardennes forest dwellers supervised bathing of newcomers as a covert mutation check, the forest rangers were respected by all, and the valley communities in the Pale Sisters were almost isolated from the outside world. His major political innovation was to move the center of his rule to Curona - which allowed him to unexpectedly solve the north-south division that previous dukes had been unable to overcome: from Curona, he was able to calmly govern North Gisoru, which had been effectively independent for centuries because of the difficult journey from the southern plains to the north. But the price was that he lost direct control of the hinterland of the plains. Another layer of complexity facing the duchy is related to the long-standing cross-river land dispute between Bastogne - some Gisorou nobles swore allegiance to the Duke of Bastogne in order to retain their fiefdoms on the other side, creating an intertwined network of cross-duchy loyalties. Hagen is approaching it all with his characteristic caution - he is not rushing to solve every problem, but is prioritizing ensuring that the principality's voice is heard on the Kurona political scene, while looking forward to time to heal those rifts that have accumulated over the centuries.
